title: Peeking Iterator
description: Brute force to optimized: draining the entire sequence upfront versus a single one-slot lookahead cache added on top of a forward-only iterator.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Design an iterator that supports the peek() operation on an existing iterator, in addition to the standard hasNext() and next() operations. peek() returns the next element WITHOUT advancing the iterator, so a subsequent next() call still returns that same element.

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An existing Iterator interface (with next() and hasNext()), wrapped by PeekingIterator"],["Output","peek() returns the next value without consuming it; next() and hasNext() behave as usual"],["Goal","Add peek() functionality using only ONE extra cached slot, without extra passes over the data"],["Constraints","At most 1000 calls to next, hasNext, and peek combined"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"View the next item without consuming it\"","A one-slot cache: pull one item ahead of time and hold onto it until next() is actually called"],["Wrapping an existing iterator interface with new functionality","The decorator pattern: wrap the existing interface, only adding the new capability on top"]]}

blocks.text: The underlying iterator only supports consuming values one at a time via next(), with no way to "look ahead" without consuming. Since there is no way to push a value back into the underlying iterator once retrieved, the PeekingIterator must retrieve and cache that value itself, only handing it off ("consuming" it) on the next actual next() call.

blocks.title: Analogy: Peeking at the Next Card in a Deck Before Drawing It
blocks.text: Picture wanting to look at the next card in a deck of cards without actually taking it out. Since the deck itself does not support "just looking," you would need to physically pull the next card, look at it, and hold onto it yourself, only handing it over as the "next draw" when actually asked.

blocks.caption: peek() caches the underlying next() call; next() drains the cache first if present

blocks.text: Example: arr = [1, 2, 3], calls = [next, peek, next, next, hasNext]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Result","Explanation"],"rows":[["next()","1","Returns 1, advances past it"],["peek()","2","Shows 2 without consuming it"],["next()","2","Returns the SAME 2 that was peeked"],["next()","3","Returns 3, the next fresh value"],["hasNext()","false","No more elements remain"]]}

blocks.text: Before trying to "look ahead" directly on the underlying iterator (which it does not support), notice that a single cached value plus a flag tracking whether that cache is currently filled is enough to implement peek() correctly on top of any next()/hasNext()-only iterator.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The underlying iterator can only be advanced forward via next(); there is no way to "undo" a next() call once made.

Observation 2: To implement peek() without consuming a value from the caller's perspective, the PeekingIterator must call the underlying next() ITSELF, and hold onto that retrieved value internally rather than handing it back to the underlying iterator.

Observation 3: A single cached slot and a boolean flag ("is there currently a peeked-but-not-yet-returned-via-next value cached?") is sufficient state to track this correctly.

Observation 4: next() must check this cache FIRST: if something is cached, return and clear it (marking it as consumed); otherwise, fall through to calling the underlying next() directly. Similarly, hasNext() should report true if either the cache holds a value OR the underlying iterator still has more.

This leads to maintaining one cached value and a flag: peek() fills the cache (calling the underlying next() if not already cached) and returns it; next() drains the cache if present, otherwise calls the underlying next() directly; hasNext() checks both the cache and the underlying iterator.

A common (but flawed) instinct is to try to make peek() and next() both call the underlying next() independently, hoping to somehow "rewind." Since the underlying iterator provides no rewind capability, a more literal "brute" approach is to eagerly materialize the ENTIRE sequence into an array upfront (using next() and hasNext() until exhausted), then implement peek/next/hasNext as simple index-based array operations.

items: Immediately drain the underlying iterator entirely into an array, calling next() until hasNext() is false.
Maintain a simple index into this array.
peek() returns the element at the current index without advancing it; next() returns it and advances; hasNext() checks if the index is still within bounds.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Materializing the whole sequence upfront sidesteps the "no rewind" limitation entirely, since everything becomes simple array indexing.
This works, but pays an unnecessary O(n) upfront cost and O(n) space, even if only a few elements are ever actually consumed.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) upfront to drain the iterator, O(1) per subsequent operation.
Space: O(n), storing the entire sequence regardless of how much is actually used.

Limitation: materializing everything upfront defeats part of the purpose of an iterator (lazy, on-demand access); a single cached slot achieves the same peek() capability without ever needing more than O(1) extra space.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why draining everything upfront is unnecessary: peek() only ever needs to look ONE element ahead, not the entire remaining sequence.

The single-slot caching trick: when peek() is called and nothing is currently cached, call the underlying next() once, store the result in a cache slot, and mark the cache as filled; return that cached value.

How next() interacts with the cache: if the cache is filled (a peek() happened since the last next()), return and clear the cached value instead of calling the underlying next() again; otherwise, call the underlying next() directly.

The core idea: exactly one item of "lookahead" state, filled lazily only when peek() is actually called, is all that is needed, preserving the lazy, on-demand nature of iteration.

Maintain a single cached value and a boolean flag. peek() fills the cache via the underlying next() if not already filled, and returns it. next() returns and clears the cache if filled, otherwise calls the underlying next() directly. hasNext() is true if the cache is filled or the underlying iterator still has elements.

blocks.caption: A single cached value and flag give peek() capability with O(1) extra space

blocks.text: Since the underlying iterator can only move forward, the PeekingIterator itself becomes the ONLY place that "remembers" a value has already been pulled but not yet officially returned via next(). The single cached slot plus flag exactly captures this state: peek() ensures something is cached (pulling ahead exactly once if needed) and returns it; next() checks the cache first (draining it if present) before ever calling the underlying next() again, guaranteeing no value is ever skipped or duplicated.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(1) for peek, next, and hasNext.
Space: O(1) extra, just the cached slot and flag.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Drain the entire iterator upfront","O(n) upfront, O(1) per call after","O(n)","Works, but defeats the lazy nature of iteration and wastes memory."],["Single cached slot, filled lazily","O(1) per call","O(1)","The expected, minimal, and idiomatic solution."]]}

blocks.text: Peeking Iterator is the canonical example of the "one-slot lookahead cache" technique for adding peek() capability to any forward-only iterator, without needing to draw more than one extra element ahead at any time.

items: Calling the underlying next() again inside next() even when a value is already cached, silently skipping an element.
Forgetting to account for the cache in hasNext(), incorrectly reporting no more elements when a peeked value is still pending.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["peek() called multiple times in a row without an intervening next()","Returns the SAME cached value every time, never advancing further."],["peek() called as the very last operation with no next() afterward","The cached value is simply never consumed, which is fine."]]}

blocks.text: Explicitly stating "since the underlying iterator cannot rewind, the wrapper itself must hold the one-item lookahead" clarifies the core design constraint driving the whole solution.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "add a look-ahead capability to a forward-only iterator", think: cache exactly one pulled-ahead value, drain it on the next real next() call.

items: How would you extend this to peek() k elements ahead instead of just 1?
How would you implement this as a generic wrapper usable with any iterator type, not just integers?
Flatten Nested List Iterator and Zigzag Iterator, other "wrap an iterator with extra behavior" design problems.
The decorator design pattern generally, wrapping an existing interface with additional capability.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The upfront-drain approach costs O(n) time and space initially; the single-cache approach costs O(1) time and space per operation, the standard idiomatic solution.

items: Pattern: a one-slot lookahead cache, wrapping a forward-only iterator to add peek() capability.
Core Idea: peek() pulls one value ahead via the underlying next() (if not already cached) and returns it; next() drains the cache first if present.
Time: O(n) upfront for the drain-everything approach, O(1) per call for the cached-slot approach.
Most Important Observation: since the underlying iterator cannot rewind, the wrapper itself must remember any value pulled ahead of time.
Interview Difficulty: a classic, accessible design problem testing careful state management around a simple cache.
One line memory trick: cache one pulled-ahead value; next() drains it first, peek() fills it if empty.
